forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton's high needs schools spending ended 2025-26 £10.4m over, against £6.8m forecast in budget
news_drafts.lead:
Spending on support for children with special educational needs in Wolverhampton ended 2025-26 at £10.4m over budget, the Schools' Forum heard on 15 October. The council's budget in February 2025 had expected an overspend of £6.8m on the "high needs" part of school funding, which covers children with special educational needs and disabilities. Spending was £62.08m against a budget of £51.72m, a 19.9% overrun.

The largest single driver was top-up payments to schools for pupils with special needs. These were £29.62m against a budget of £26.91m, an overspend of £2.72m, or 10%. The paper says the increase was part of the overspend already indicated at the third quarter. Within top-up funding, special schools and alternative provision (education outside mainstream schools) took £1.9m of additional spend, and exceptional needs funding, for specialist equipment and one-to-one support, rose £340,000, or 15%, on the previous year. Independent provision for under-16s within the city ran £0.83m (17%) over, at £5.70m against £4.87m. Provision outside the city came in £0.61m (7%) under.

Other parts of the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) partly offset the overspend. The Schools Block had a £0.5m surplus and the Early Years Block a £0.4m underspend. The net deficit held in the council's unusable reserve for the grant stood at £9.2m at year-end, up £4.3m from £4.9m a year earlier.

news_drafts.headline: West Midlands Pension Fund misses member benefit statement deadline
news_drafts.lead: The West Midlands Pension Fund was unable to issue annual benefit statements to all members by the statutory deadline of 31 August 2025. By August 2026, only 80 per cent of active and 93 per cent of deferred members had received statements, auditors found. The fund had self-reported the issue to the Pensions Regulator. Auditors also identified £20.7m in unadjusted investment valuations that management will not correct and £14.1m in early retirement costs recorded in the wrong financial year. Member records also contained discrepancies. Despite these issues, the fund's total assets grew by £1.2bn to £24.6bn in the quarter ending 30 June, and investment management costs fell to 0.41 per cent of assets.

news_drafts.headline: Wolverhampton Council repaid £17m in loans to avoid proposed rate increases of up to 6.26% on LOBO facilities
news_drafts.lead: Wolverhampton Council rejected proposals to increase rates on three bank loans totaling £17m and chose instead to repay them in full. LOBO loans are bank loans where lenders can propose new terms on set dates. Between July 2025 and January 2026, a £7m Commerzbank loan came with a proposed rate of 6.19%, compared with its existing 3.60%; two £5m Dexia loans proposed 6.21% and 6.26%, against existing rates of 4.26% and 4.29%. According to the Treasury Management Annual Report, this refinancing required £17m in cash but protected the council from substantially higher day-to-day running costs.

findings.paper_title: Schools' Forum DFC Balances Update Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: 11 schools exceeded three-year Devolved Formula Capital holding limit by £110,926 as at 31 August 2026, risking DfE clawback
findings.detail: Eleven schools had exceeded the three-year limit for holding Devolved Formula Capital as at 31 August 2026, with overly-aged balances totalling £110,926. The council has advised these schools of the risk that the DfE may claw back excess balances. Overall, the council's combined balance was within the allowable total, so no immediate clawback is applicable.
findings.matters: Unspent capital funding may be reclaimed by the funder; managing capital spending to avoid clawback is a resource governance duty
findings.figures: 11 schools, £110,926 in overly-aged balances, three-year allowance threshold
findings.quote: 11 schools are carrying balances of DFC that had exceeded three years as at 31 August 2026 and the total of this element of the DFC is £110,926.

findings.paper_title: Schools' Forum DFC Balances Update Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Excess school surplus balances decreased by £786,000 to £8.8 million; 20 schools exceed permitted thresholds, down from 24 in prior year
findings.detail: The council actively manages schools' excess surpluses through written inquiry. The total excess surplus fell from £9.6 million (24 schools) in 2024-2025 to £8.8 million (20 schools) in 2025-2026. All 20 schools holding excess surpluses submitted responses to the council's 11 September 2026 deadline. Current financial information indicates school balances will reduce further in 2026-2027.
findings.matters: Excess surpluses represent unused capacity or inefficient resource deployment; active management of these is a governance indicator
findings.figures: £8.8 million total (down from £9.6 million); 20 schools exceeding thresholds (down from 24); changes by type: Nurseries +£43,000, Primary -£287,000, Secondary -£1.03 million, Special +£491,000
findings.quote: The total excess surplus balances have decreased overall by £786,000 from a total of £9.6 million reported in 2024-2025 to £8.8million in 2025-2026.

findings.paper_title: Schools' Forum DFC Balances Update Report 2025-2026
findings.headline: Two schools entered deficit for first time in 2025-2026; eight schools in deficit with external support programme temporarily suspended
findings.detail: Eight schools reported deficits in 2025-2026, including two entering deficit for the first time and four in ongoing recovery from prior-year deficits. Four schools in recovery received support from the DfE's Schools Resource Management Advisory Programme (SRMA) in summer 2026; however, the DfE has temporarily suspended the SRMA programme while considering a new approach. The council will provide direct support to the two newly-identified deficit schools.
findings.matters: School deficits consume council resources; suspension of external support adds pressure on the council's capacity to manage recovery
findings.figures: 8 schools in deficit at 31 March 2026: 2 new entries, 4 in ongoing recovery, 2 in existing monitoring recovery; SRMA advisor visits in summer 2026, programme now temporarily suspended
findings.quote: Of the eight schools reporting a deficit in 2025-2026, two schools are in a deficit position for the first time.

findings.headline: In-City independent SEND provision for Pre-16 pupils increased 17% while out-of-city provision fell 7%
findings.detail: In-City independent provision for Pre-16 SEND pupils overran by £0.83m (17% increase), from £4.87m budgeted to £5.70m spent. This was partially offset by a £0.61m underspend (7% fall) in out-of-city Pre-16 provision, leaving independent settings with a net £0.19m overspend.
findings.matters: A shift toward in-city placements indicates either changing pupil needs or market dynamics in independent provision. In-city provision is typically more costly than out-of-city, so a shift signals rising placement costs and a changing budget dynamic.
findings.figures: In-city: budget £4.87m, outturn £5.70m, overspend £0.83m (17%); out-of-city: budget £8.32m, outturn £7.70m, underspend £0.61m (7%)

findings.headline: Alternative Provision (placements and inclusion) increased 43% against budget
findings.detail: Alternative Provision – placements in alternative educational settings and inclusion support – was budgeted at £0.76m but spent £1.08m, an overspend of £0.33m. At 43% over budget, this is the highest percentage increase in the High Needs Block.
findings.matters: A 43% increase in alternative provision suggests rising demand for out-of-school placements or inclusion support, potentially reflecting growing numbers of pupils who cannot be managed in mainstream or SEND schools, signalling emerging capacity pressure.

daily_post.headline: Current assets in the pension fund fell 47% in the quarter, from £88.8m to £47.1m, with no explanation provided
daily_post.lead: A sharp quarterly decline in liquid current assets may indicate cash flow timing or reflect working capital reductions that the council or a lender would need to understand, particularly if it signals liquidity pressures or changes in fund management
